passages.original: Si. Inter Ice Ius et facinus hoc interest, quod scelus crimen est, facinus etiam in laude recte dici- tur; Sallustius dicit bonum facinus,
passages.english: Between *scelus* [crime] and *facinus* [deed] there is this difference: *scelus* is a crime, whereas *facinus* is also correctly used in praise; Sallust says "a good deed" (*bonum facinus*).
passages.notes: "Si. Inter Ice Ius" is a scanning error; read "Inter scelus" (the leading "Si." is probably a misread section number). The Latin pair scelus/facinus is kept in italics since the distinction depends on the words. The passage breaks off after the Sallust example.

passages.original: Inter geminatum, junctumet duplicatum quid intersit quamvis acute intelligentibus breviter exposuerimus, tamen sub exemplis latius doceamus. Geminatum est quod ex duabus rebus similibus constat, ut Cicero: Gemina audacia. Junctum est quod ex duabus rebusparibus constat, ut Virgilius : Jungentur jam gryphes equi. Duplicatum est cum una res bis ponitur : Ingens ad terram .duplicato poplite.
passages.english: Although we have briefly set out, for those of keen understanding, what the difference is between *geminatum* [twinned], *junctum* [joined] and *duplicatum* [doubled], let us nevertheless teach it more fully with examples. *Geminatum* is what consists of two similar things, as Cicero [says]: "twin audacity." *Junctum* is what consists of two equal things, as Virgil [says]: "Now griffins will be joined with horses." *Duplicatum* is when one thing is put twice: "huge, to the ground, with doubled knee."
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "junctumet" = "junctum et", "rebusparibus" = "rebus paribus", "gryphes equi" (Virgil reads "gryphes equis"). The last quotation is Virgil (Aeneid 12) of a warrior falling with knee bent double; Isidore gives no author for it.

passages.original: 182. Inter hostiam et victimam hoc interest, quod hostia perhibetur tunc , cum dux in hostes proficiscitur; victima, cum vincti, sicut Ovidius in Fast.: Victima quæ cecidit dextra victrice vocatur. Hostibus a domitis hostia nomen habet.
passages.english: Between *hostia* and *victima* [both, sacrificial victim] there is this difference: it is called *hostia* when the commander sets out against the enemy (*hostes*); *victima*, when [the enemy have been] conquered (*victi*), as Ovid [says] in the Fasti: "The victim that falls by the victorious right hand is called *victima*; from enemies (*hostes*) subdued the *hostia* takes its name."
passages.notes: "vincti" (bound) in the text is probably a scanning error or variant for "victi" (conquered), which the etymology requires; translated as "victi". "a domitis" read as "ab domitis"/"a domitis". Latin terms are kept because the point is etymological.
